title: AI-experiments in education: An AI-driven randomized controlled trial for higher education research
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI can be used not only as a data-collection tool but also as the engine for running a fully automated double-blind randomized controlled trial in higher education research. The authors focus on a methodological problem: how to conduct causal experiments efficiently and at scale using an AI chatbot without human intervention during participant interaction, allocation, and data capture.

The intervention was an AI-led chatbot survey built with IBM Watson Assistant (named Sydn-E), which randomly assigned participants to one control group or one of eight experimental groups. Each experimental group received the same base university description plus a different positive eWOM prompt about a university attribute: reputation/ranking, cost/scholarships, work placements/job prospects, admissions ease, campus location, course/support services, prior knowledge of the destination, or collaboration with other universities. The outcome was participants’ likelihood of enrolling in the hypothetical university, measured on a 5-point Likert scale. The study used Welch two-sample t-tests and Mann-Whitney U tests to compare each experimental condition with the control.

The sample consisted of 1,193 recruited participants from Prolific, globally distributed, aged 18–30, all of whom had completed high school, used at least one social media platform, and were native English speakers. The paper presents the study as a higher-education decision-making experiment rather than a direct instructional intervention. It argues that the AI system successfully handled blind allocation, conducted the survey, rejected low-quality responses, and generated structured data for analysis.

The main findings were that five of the eight tested factors significantly increased students’ reported likelihood of enrolling: reputation/ranking, cost/scholarships, work and internship opportunities, campus location, and course/support services. Admissions ease, prior knowledge of the destination, and collaboration with other universities were not statistically supported. The authors conclude that AI can serve as a rigorous, scalable platform for RCTs in education research, though the study is primarily a demonstration of method rather than an instructional effectiveness trial.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial with random allocation and blinding, which is strong for causal inference. However, it is an educational research-methods study rather than a direct student outcome trial, and the intervention is a chatbot-mediated experimental platform rather than a conventional educational treatment, so there are some relevance/construct concerns.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed effects on enrolment intention were modest-to-moderate and statistically significant in five of eight conditions, with no reported standardized effect sizes. The broader impact is promising for institutional research efficiency and for understanding university-choice messaging, but it does not yet demonstrate direct learning gains.

interventions.use_case: AI-led chatbot interview-like survey (IBM Watson Assistant 'Sydn-E') that automatically randomized participants, delivered condition-specific prompts, collected responses, and administered a double-blind online RCT in higher education research.

finding.finding_summary: This RCT tested whether positive electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) about university attributes increased students' likelihood of enrolling in a hypothetical university. Compared with the control group (n=144), five experimental conditions showed statistically significant increases in enrolment likelihood: EG1 (n=136, t=-4.774, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.747, -0.311]), EG2 (n=144, t=-3.444, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.566, -0.154]), EG3 (n=135, t=-4.482, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.647, -0.252]), EG5 (n=132, t=-3.548, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.588, -0.168]), and EG6 (n=130, t=-3.681, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.595, -0.180]). The outcome was a 5-point Likert-scale enrolment intention measure in a hypothetical university-choice scenario.
finding.measure: Likelihood to enrol in a university (5-point Likert scale)

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily demonstrates an institutional research-methods intervention: an AI system that fully automated recruitment, allocation, interviewing, and data capture for a double-blind online RCT. The platform processed 1,193 participants and rejected 30 submissions (2.45%) for inconsistency or inadequate input, showing feasibility for scalable higher-education experimentation rather than direct student learning gains.
finding.measure: RCT automation feasibility; participant allocation, response validation, and data collection quality
